paragraphs: Many girls in Ireland do not feel sure about their skills in science and maths. A new survey shows this.
The survey asked more than 2,300 girls in primary and secondary schools.

Six in ten girls said a lack of confidence stops them from choosing a Stem job. Stem means science, technology, engineering and maths. Last year the number was 55%. In 2024 it was 50%. Many girls also said they do not get enough information about Stem jobs.
Many girls' schools do not teach computer science. Only 27% of girls in these schools can study it.
The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said Ireland needs more women in digital jobs.
More and more girls are losing confidence in their ability in Stem subjects, a new survey has found. Stem stands for science, technology, engineering and maths.

The I Wish survey was answered by 1,660 primary students and 662 secondary students. Researchers at University College Cork studied the results. I Wish is a programme that encourages teenage girls to choose Stem careers.

Six in ten girls said that a lack of confidence was a barrier to a Stem career. This has risen from 55% last year and 50% in 2024. Two-thirds of girls also said that gender inequality and a lack of information about Stem jobs were problems.
The survey also found big differences between schools. Only 27% of girls in girls-only schools can study computer science for the Leaving Cert, compared with over 60% in mixed schools.
Women now make up 36% of Stem students at university, up from 31% in 2018. But only one in five digital workers is a woman. Taoiseach Micheál Martin said fixing this was important for the economy.
A growing number of girls lack confidence in their ability in science, technology, engineering and maths (Stem), according to a new survey.

The I Wish survey of 1,660 primary and 662 secondary students was analysed by psychology researchers at University College Cork. I Wish runs a programme that encourages teenage girls to pursue careers in Stem.

Some 60% of respondents said a lack of confidence in their Stem ability was a barrier to a career in the field, up from 55% in 2025 and 50% in 2024. Two-thirds identified gender inequality and a lack of information about Stem careers as significant obstacles.

The report also highlights uneven access to subjects. Only 27% of girls in single-sex schools can take computer science for the Leaving Cert, compared with more than 60% in mixed schools, and practical subjects such as engineering are far less available.

Women's share of Stem undergraduate places rose from 31% in 2018 to 36% last year, but women make up only a fifth of digital specialists. Speaking at the launch, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said tackling this imbalance was essential for the economy.
A mounting proportion of girls doubt their aptitude in science, technology, engineering and maths (Stem), a new survey has found.

The I Wish survey, which canvassed 1,660 primary and 662 secondary students, was analysed by psychology researchers at University College Cork. I Wish runs a programme designed to steer teenage girls towards Stem careers.

Some 60% of respondents cited a lack of self-belief in their Stem ability as an impediment to pursuing a career in the field, up from 55% in 2025 and 50% in 2024. Two-thirds singled out gender inequality and a dearth of career information as formidable obstacles.

The report also flags stark disparities in subject provision. A mere 27% of girls in single-sex schools have access to Leaving Cert computer science, against upwards of 60% in co-educational schools, while hands-on subjects such as engineering are markedly scarcer.

Although women's share of Stem undergraduate places has edged up from 31% in 2018 to 36%, they comprise only a fifth of the digital specialist workforce. At the launch, Taoiseach Micheál Martin stressed that redressing this imbalance was indispensable to cultivating the talent the economy requires.
An increasing proportion of girls lack confidence in their abilities in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Stem), according to a recently published survey.

The I Wish survey, which gathered responses from 1,660 primary and 662 secondary students, was analysed by psychology researchers at University College Cork. I Wish operates a programme intended to encourage teenage girls to pursue Stem careers.

Approximately 60% of respondents identified a lack of confidence in their Stem ability as a barrier to a career in the field, compared with 55% in 2025 and 50% in 2024. Furthermore, two-thirds regarded gender inequality and insufficient information about Stem careers as substantial obstacles.

The report also underlines considerable disparities in subject availability. Only 27% of girls in single-sex schools have access to computer science at Leaving Cert level, whereas the figure exceeds 60% in mixed schools; moreover, practical subjects such as engineering are considerably less accessible in single-sex schools.

Although the proportion of women in Stem undergraduate programmes increased from 31% in 2018 to 36%, women nevertheless constitute merely one fifth of the digital specialist workforce. At the launch, Taoiseach Micheál Martin emphasised that addressing this imbalance is essential to developing the talent upon which the economy depends.
